Introduction (p. 85) as stated. Table 1 checked at 300 dpi: blotters for 25N, 25E, 25G, 25D, 25I (with powder), 25B, 25H, 25B-N(BOMe)2 (8); powder only 25C, 25iP (2); police or customs; January 2011 to June 2013.

results.corrected_extracted: Cases in which people believed they had taken LSD: a 24-year-old woman at the Burning Man festival had taken 'acid' on blotter paper, whose remains held mainly 25C-NBOMe and a very small amount of 25I-NBOMe; her own samples were not analysed. Three people in Belgium, brought to hospital from the same party, reported using 'synthetic LSD'; 25I-NBOMe was confirmed in their urine, with no other drugs detected. A 21-year-old man in Houston who reportedly had taken two 'hits of acid' and smoked cannabis hallucinated, reportedly injured himself, attacked a friend, and was found unresponsive; 25I-NBOMe and cannabis metabolites were found in his post-mortem heart blood and urine. A 19-year-old in Richmond, Virginia, 'trip sitting' friends who were reportedly using 'acid', behaved strangely and was found after probably jumping or falling from a balcony; a case-related sample of unused blotter paper held 25I-NBOMe and targeted analysis found it in his blood, urine, brain, liver and bile; his friends did not know he had taken anything, and those who took the 'acid' blotters showed no similar symptoms. In Belgium a person had used a blotter at a party that they thought contained LSD; no LSD was found, and analytical confirmation of 25I-NBOMe was not reported.
results.note: All facts and locations hold. The Houston case is hedged in the source ('it is reported that he took two hits of acid', 'it is reported that he self-injured'); 'reportedly' restored.

Abstract, Acute toxicity paragraph 1 and Conclusions as stated. Recount of the 29 case descriptions: seizures 12 (37.9% = 11/29), acute kidney injury 6, ages 14-31, 17 men of 19 with sex given; all agree.

pp. 87-89 and Table 2 (300 dpi): status epilepticus, 40°C, day 6; German case self-reported, haemofiltration, ventilation, day 13; Grand Rapids 3 of 4 intubated, CK 30,000, haemodialysis; Hill case 1 38 days ICU, 43 days; cases 3-7 15 h to under 24 h.
p. 90 poison-centre paragraph: 25 cases (8, 17), 19 (76%), 3 (12%), 3 unidentified, 21 (84%), 52/48/32/32/24/20%, seizures 4% against 38%. 4% of 25 is 1: recomputed.

Abstract and the ten death paragraphs (pp. 90-91): five deaths with detection and three without (Australia via media and family report, first Belgian, Polish), matrices and co-detected substances as stated; 5 + 3 = the abstract's eight.

results.corrected_extracted: Editors' count from the case descriptions: the NBOMe was found in the patient's own samples, with the result linked to the patient, in 15 of the 29 published cases (both Hong Kong cases, the Richmond 25B-NBOMe case, the seven Hill cases, the Richmond 25I-NBOMe case, the St Paul case and three of the four Grand Rapids cases); only the product was analysed in 2 (Detroit, Burning Man); no analysis linked to the patient was reported in 12 (the German 25C-NBOMe case, the ten Richmond patients, whose two analysed serum samples could not be linked to patients, and one Grand Rapids patient). Other drugs found or reported include amphetamine and methamphetamine in six of the seven Hill cases, ketamine in the second Hong Kong case, caffeine in three Grand Rapids cases, a substance thought to be a phencyclidine analogue in the Detroit eye dropper, and co-use reported by four of the ten Richmond patients. The Conclusions say only some reports included analytical confirmation, read the features as both serotonin syndrome and sympathomimetic toxicity, much like MDMA, certain other amphetamines and mephedrone, and say the significance of post-mortem detection for the deaths has often not been determined.
results.note: Counts 15 + 2 + 12 = 29 recomputed and correct; Table 3 (B: n/a) and Hill urine and plasma agree. Only change: the third eye-dropper substance 'was thought to be' a PCP analogue (p. 88).

Prevalence paragraphs 2-4 (pp. 86-87): 22,289, 582 (2.6%), LSD 8,774 (39.4%), 397, 4.8% against 76.6%; ref. 19 (Clin Toxicol 2014;52:361) falls in the EAPCCT 2014 abstracts (ref. 8, pp. 295-443). Declaration of interest (p. 91) as stated.

key_findings.note: Finding as stated. In the note, the regular-use bar of Figure 6 measures about 23% at 300 dpi (card: 24%), within reading error.

key_findings.correction: Among veteran addicts (men addicted in Vietnam) who returned to narcotics, the variables in Table 2 failed to predict re-addiction: behaviour problems before service; parents' substance abuse, arrest or psychiatric care; substance use in Vietnam (types, duration, injection); IQ; draftee or volunteer; combat; military discipline problems; demographic characteristics. The text says the social and behavioural variables that had explained who became addicted in Vietnam and which ex-addicts used again after return were of no use in explaining which relapsers became re-addicted. The author suggests vulnerability to re-addiction may be biological, saying it is not known whether it is present from birth or created by the drug, and that different factors operate at each transition (to use, to addiction, to remission, to relapse).
key_findings.note: The card says 'veterans' (Table 2: veteran addicts), 'parents' substance use' (Table 2: substance abuse), and that the listed variables had predicted use in Vietnam; combat, for one, had not (p. 1049).

key_findings.correction: Other studies cited as consistent: 50 untreated people free of heroin addiction for at least 2 years had a median addiction of 5.7 years (Waldorf & Biernacki, 1979); among young men 18-28 registered with Selective Service, 13% of those reporting heroin use had been treated, and 27% of the untreated against 65% of the treated had used heroin in the past year (O'Donnell et al., 1976); 25% of Harlem youths aged 18-23 who had used heroin twice or more had used it in the current year, 16% of the untreated (Brunswick, 1979); in the ECA, substance abuse had the shortest mean duration of any psychiatric disorder, 2.7 years (estimated from ages at first and last problem), and only one in five people dependent on or abusing an illicit drug had had any treatment; most of these cases were not heroin addicts (marijuana was the most common drug of abuse).
key_findings.note: The source says most ECA cases were not heroin addicts; the card's 'most of them not for heroin' reads as most of the treated being treated for other drugs.

reporting_issues.note: Figure 8 measured at 300 dpi: year-1 addicts about 30% addicted, 50% users, 20% abstainers in years 2-3.
Figure 1 measured at 300 dpi: about 93, 74-75, 40, 36, 24-25 and 23-24%.
Figure 9 measured: about 34.5% and 2% in a drug facility, 42.5% and 28.6% only other care.

risk_of_bias.note: Design narrative-review (a lecture reviewing the author's own cohort), instrument none-applicable with the editors' checklist, overall high (worst domains: no search, reliance on own studies): all agreed.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible: the data-based statements stay within the data and opinions are marked as hers. The weakest step, the 'not unique' answer resting on indirect civilian studies, is already set out in 'claimed'.

missed: sample.recruitment: 13,280 was the researchers' own estimate of September returnees; the Department of Defense's later revised estimate, from the planes' lading documents, came within 3% of it (p. 1043). The card says the true number was later estimated at 13,280.

Context for the treatment findings: the only rise in VA cases came from a DoD rule delaying discharge by 30 days, spent by drug-positive soldiers in a VA drug programme; they arrived already detoxified and in no obvious need of treatment (p. 1048).

Item (6), Zinberg and Jacobson's 'chippers' (recreational heroin users who never became addicted), is cited (p. 1050) but appears nowhere on the card; the gap text counts six supporting studies where design_detail counts seven.
The first interviews were all completed within 6 months, after a funding delay of 8 months (pp. 1042-1043): the source of the 8-12-month window in reporting issue 2.

key_findings.note: Recount agrees: seizures 12, agitation 17, kidney injury 6, tachycardia 28 of 29.

key_findings.correction: Severe complications among the published cases included status epilepticus with a rectal temperature of 40°C (25B-NBOMe), rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury (peak creatine kinase up to 30,000 IU/L; haemofiltration in one case, haemodialysis in two), acute lung injury needing prolonged invasive ventilation (self-reported 25C-NBOMe, with no analysis of samples or product), and a 38-day intensive-care stay after intravenous injection of a liquid labelled 25I-NBOMe, followed by discharge after 43 days with normal kidney function.
key_findings.note: The 25C case is self-reported only; the review says it cannot be certain the features were due to 25C-NBOMe (p. 88).

key_findings.correction: Ten patients aged 14-20 in Richmond, Virginia (congress abstract), after swallowing or snorting '25-I': tachycardia in 9, hypertension 7, agitation 6, hallucinations 5, prolonged seizures 2, reduced consciousness 1; one with prolonged seizures had 'discrete intraparenchymal haemorrhages' (the review names no organ) and acute kidney injury; six were admitted to intensive care for observation. No analysis was reported in the abstract; serum from two patients, later analysed, contained 25I-NBOMe but could not be linked to particular patients.
key_findings.note: Minor: 'within the brain' is not in the review.

key_findings.correction: Several deaths followed disturbed behaviour: a 17-year-old in Australia was reported to act erratically and then jumped from a third-floor balcony; a 19-year-old in Richmond, 'trip sitting' friends who were reportedly using 'acid' and not known by them to have taken anything, probably jumped or fell from a balcony; a case-related sample of unused blotter paper contained 25I-NBOMe, and it was confirmed in his samples; a 21-year-old in Houston who reportedly had taken two 'hits of acid' hallucinated, reportedly injured himself and attacked a friend before being found unresponsive. A 15-year-old who drank an unknown clear liquid was in asystole and hyperthermic (39.9°C) on arrival. The post-mortem examinations of the two Houston deaths showed only external injuries.
key_findings.note: The review does not say the friends' blotters held 25I-NBOMe (only 'a case-related sample of non-ingested blotter paper'); 'probably' and the Houston 'it is reported' hedges restored (pp. 90-91).

key_findings.correction: How NBOMes were sold or mistaken: typically on blotters, also as powder and liquid. People in several cases believed they had taken LSD: a woman at the Burning Man festival had taken 'acid' on blotter paper whose remains contained mainly 25C-NBOMe with a very small amount of 25I-NBOMe; the three Belgian cases reported 'synthetic LSD'; a man who died in Houston reportedly had taken two 'hits of acid'; a Belgian who died had used a blotter believed to contain LSD, and no LSD was found; in Richmond, where friends were reportedly using 'acid', a case-related sample of unused blotter paper contained 25I-NBOMe. Other forms: a liquid labelled 25I-NBOMe from a dealer, capsules bought online, an 'NBOMe' pill, a sublingual 'Holland film', and an eye dropper said to hold 2C-T-2 or 2C-T-7 that held two 2C-NBOMe variants and a substance thought to be a PCP analogue. By the editors' count of Table 1 (p. 86), 8 of the 10 first detections in Europe in 2011-2013 were on blotters, alone or with powder.
key_findings.note: Same Richmond blotter inference and Houston hedge as finding 11; the PCP analogue was only 'thought to be' one (p. 88).

key_findings.correction: The review describes 25I-NBOMe as a very potent 5-HT2A receptor agonist (Ki 0.044-0.15, printed in nm), with reported amounts taken lower than for other new psychoactive substances such as mephedrone and similar to those of other potent hallucinogens such as LSD.
key_findings.note: The source says 'lower than', not 'far smaller' (p. 85).

reporting_issues.note: Table 2 at 300 dpi: cases 4, 6, 7 at 37.3, 36.5, 36.9°C marked Yes.

risk_of_bias.note: Narrative review, editors' checklist (none-applicable); a search is described but selection is not explicit; some concerns in every domain and overall: agreed.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the abstract's eight detections (five in the body), five kidney injuries (six described) and the prevalence conclusion from non-representative surveys, against a cautious body.

missed: exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: 'far smaller than for mephedrone' overstates the review's 'lower than' (p. 85); 'sublingual (a film, blotter)': no sublingual blotter is described (the St Paul case's form is not stated; the Burning Man blotters were 'ingested').
